analysis.title: Market Musings 11/26: Data centres: life after mid-terms
key_insights: The US mid-terms put data centres and electricity affordability at the center of many campaigns, which affects new data centre build-out and the listed US utilities positioned for higher electricity demand growth.
After the Democratic sweep, the firm does not expect the data centre build-out to end. It expects a more nuanced build-out that favors active, bottom-up investors.

The EIA expects average US residential electricity prices to rise 10.5% between 2024 and 2026, almost double the 5.8% rise in consumer prices. Rising bills are increasing local opposition to data centres (NIMBY).

The firm overlays Fractracker Alliance data on organised opposition to data centres onto its asset maps. This shows which data centre operators and electric utilities most need to address local opposition.
Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a data centre moratorium. It applies mostly to planned projects, not those already operating or under construction.

The moratorium is not a full stop. Planned data centres must disclose their electricity and water use and their supplier to move past planning. The firm sees this as sensible, and it gives utilities more control over tariffs.

Utilities can use separate pricing for residential customers and large-load customers (data centres, industrial, commercial). Some utilities under the firm's coverage use data centre charges to subsidise residential electricity costs.
The firm selects listed utilities that already have a large-load tariff framework, either self-designed or state-mandated. It prioritises this check in the areas with the most opposition.

The firm adds its own affordability analysis, which measures electricity bills as a share of income in each service area and the rate of increase. This tests whether a utility's pricing framework goes far enough, and it feeds into valuation.
The firm does not see the mid-terms as the end of the AI theme. It sees the start of more regulation and a shift in power from data centres toward utilities.

sector_views.rationale: Utilities with large-load tariff frameworks gain pricing control as regulation shifts power from data centres toward utilities. The report does not state an explicit overweight rating, so this is inferred from its stock-selection approach.

macro_indicators.indicator: US average residential electricity price change, 2024-2026
macro_indicators.interpretation: Residential bills are rising nearly twice as fast as consumer prices, which fuels political pressure on data centre build-out.
This is the benchmark the report uses to show that electricity prices are rising faster than general inflation.

risk_factors: Local opposition (NIMBY) to data centres is growing as electricity bills rise.
Moratoriums on planned data centres, as proposed in Texas, could slow new build-out.
Utilities without a large-load tariff framework are more exposed to political and regulatory pressure over residential bills.
geopolitical: US mid-term elections ended in a Democratic sweep, with data centres and affordability as campaign issues.
Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa promised a moratorium on data centres.

key_data_points.metric: Expected rise in average US residential electricity prices, 2024 to 2026
key_data_points.context: Almost double the 5.8% increase in consumer prices over the same period.
key_data_points.anchor: average US residential electricity prices are expected to rise 10.5% between 2024 and 2026

key_data_points.metric: Increase in US consumer prices, 2024 to 2026
key_data_points.context: Compared with the 10.5% expected rise in residential electricity prices.
key_data_points.anchor: almost double the 5.8% increase in consumer prices

tension_points.bull_case: Regulation is sensible, not a halt. Disclosure requirements shift power toward utilities, which gain control over tariffs. A more nuanced build-out gives bottom-up stock pickers opportunities.
tension_points.bear_case: Affordability concerns and NIMBY opposition, with moratoriums such as the one proposed in Texas, could slow new data centre build-out after the Democratic sweep.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A planned data centre moving past planning without disclosing its electricity use, water use and named utility supplier would undercut the view that regulation shifts power to utilities.

theme_stances.key_argument: More sensible regulation shifts power from data centres toward utilities and creates opportunities for bottom-up stock pickers.
theme_stances.evidence: a further shift in power from data centres towards utilities
